vignette:
Tariq Mansour is a 41-year-old Syrian-American professional dancer and choreographer who presents to outpatient therapy reporting significant and persistent psychological distress following his experience as a civilian during the siege of his hometown in northwestern Syria approximately four years ago. He emigrated to the United States shortly thereafter and now lives with his wife in a mid-sized American city, where he teaches contemporary dance at a performing arts studio. His PCL-5 score of 58 places him firmly within the severe range of PTSD symptomatology, and his presentation reflects a man who has managed, through considerable effort, to maintain the outward structure of a functioning life while privately feeling that something essential in him has been extinguished.

The events that brought Tariq to this point unfolded over several weeks during an intense period of aerial bombardment. He had stayed behind in his neighborhood longer than most, helping elderly relatives prepare to evacuate, when a strike hit a building two streets away. He remembers the particular quality of the sound - not a single explosion but a sequence, a low concussive thud followed by the prolonged collapse of masonry, a sound that seemed to travel through the ground before it reached his ears. He ran toward the rubble with several other men, and what he recalls most viscerally is the smell of turned earth and pulverized concrete, a smell that was everywhere in the weeks that followed as buildings continued to fall, as the ground was repeatedly broken open. He lost a close friend in those weeks, a man named Samir, whose name he heard called out by search teams over and over in the dust and smoke. He eventually left, but he has never been certain he was right to do so.

In the years since arriving in the United States, Tariq's symptoms have developed and calcified in ways he finds difficult to articulate but impossible to ignore. Sounds carry a particular weight for him now. At the studio where he teaches, the bass frequencies of music played in an adjacent rehearsal room - the kind of low, rolling vibration that travels through the floor - can stop him mid-sentence, his body momentarily elsewhere. Construction noise from a nearby building project has made certain afternoons nearly unworkable; he has rearranged his teaching schedule twice to avoid the hours when drilling is most frequent, telling colleagues it is a matter of acoustics. On one occasion, a student's father introduced himself as Samir, and Tariq found he could not finish the conversation, excusing himself to the bathroom where he stood at the sink until his hands stopped shaking. He has not been able to fully explain to his wife why certain evenings he returns from work hollowed out in a way that has nothing to do with fatigue.

What troubles Tariq most, in the quiet of his own reasoning, is not the disruption these moments cause but what he has come to believe they reveal. He is certain, in a way he cannot argue himself out of, that the damage is visible on him - that when parents drop their children off at the studio, when colleagues greet him in the hallway, they are registering something wrong in his face or his bearing, some mark of what he witnessed. He has stopped attending the small social gatherings his wife organizes, and she has noticed. He has also lost something he once considered foundational: a sense that the world holds any coherent meaning, that people are essentially trustworthy, that the faith he was raised with offers any real orientation. He describes feeling dead inside - not sad, he is careful to say, but absent, as though the emotional register that once made dancing feel like communication has gone quiet.

It was his wife who finally insisted he speak to someone, after he declined an invitation to perform at a community event - something he would once have embraced - without offering any explanation. Tariq came to the first session guarded but present. What he fears most is that nothing will change, that this is simply who he is now. What he hopes, though he holds it tentatively, is that he might find a way back to the person who once believed that movement could mean something.
